claim: The deduction for interest on loans for new, U.S.-assembled passenger vehicles (up to $10,000 of interest a year, available to non-itemizers, phasing out above $100,000 / $200,000 MAGI) applies only to tax years 2025 through 2028. At the latest average commercial-bank rate for a 60-month new-car loan (7.14%, May 2026), a $10,000 loan carries $1,920 of interest over its life. If payments start in January 2026, 82.5% of that interest falls in deductible years; starting January 2027, 61.9%; starting January 2028, 34.3%. For a borrower in the 12% bracket, a loan starting in 2026 saves about $190 per $10,000 borrowed - the same total cost as a loan at about 6.47% with no deduction, i.e. about 0.67 percentage point off the rate (22% bracket: about 5.90%, 1.24 points). For a loan starting in 2028 the equivalent rate is about 6.86% in the 12% bracket (0.28 point) and 6.63% in the 22% bracket. Sources: 26 U.S.C. 163(h)(4), 63(b)(7); FRED RIFLPBCIANM60NM (Federal Reserve G.19).

assumptions: Eligible loan: new, U.S.-assembled vehicle for personal use, first lien, originated after 2024; MAGI below the phase-out; interest well under the $10,000 cap.
Rate = latest monthly average for 60-month new-car loans at commercial banks; individual rates differ (dealer/captive financing, credit score).

provisions.quote: In the case of taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029, for purposes of this subsection

means any interest which is paid or accrued during the taxable year on indebtedness incurred by the taxpayer after December 31, 2024, for the purchase of, and that is secured by a first lien on, an applicable passenger vehicle for personal use.
for any taxable year shall not exceed $10,000.

shall be reduced (but not below zero) by $200 for each $1,000 (or portion thereof) by which the modified adjusted gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year exceeds $100,000 ($200,000 in the case of a joint return).
Such term shall not include any vehicle the final assembly of which did not occur within the United States.
so much of the deduction allowed by section 163(a) as is attributable to the exception under section 163(h)(4)(A)
